explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says they're like “…servants waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet…” (Luke 12:36). It's like leaving the porch light on for someone you love, except these servants are also dressed and ready to go. Nobody's waiting for anyone else in these verses.

No vineyard owner's son shows up anywhere in these verses, friend. That sounds like a different story. Here, Jesus says the servants are waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet (Luke 12:36). The whole picture is about staying ready for him.

There's no Samaritan in these verses, baker. Jesus says the servants are waiting for their master, who's coming back from a wedding banquet (Luke 12:36). It's his knock they're ready for. The whole picture is about staying ready for him.
Yes, baker! Jesus says the servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). No digging for keys, no yelling 'one minute!' through the door. Ready servants just open up.

Dawn isn't the word here, friend. Jesus says the ready servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). He even says the master might come in the second or third watch of the night (Luke 12:38). So ready servants don't wait around for a certain hour.

Noon isn't the word here, baker. Jesus says the servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). The master might even show up in the second or third watch of the night (Luke 12:38). So ready servants don't wait around for a certain hour.

explanations.answer: He waits on them at the table
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus says, “…he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.” (Luke 12:37). The master is the one doing the serving. I've been serving cookies a long time, and I've never seen that coming either.

explanations.answer: He gives each one a bag of silver
explanations.explanation: No silver is mentioned in these verses, baker. What Jesus says is better than a bag. The master “…will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.” (Luke 12:37). The master is the one doing the serving.

explanations.answer: He lets them sleep until morning
explanations.explanation: A nap sounds nice, friend, but that's not what Jesus describes. The master finds them on watch, and then he has them recline at the table. Jesus says “…he himself will come and wait on them.” (Luke 12:37). Sleeping in never comes up.

True, baker! Jesus says, “Even if he comes in the second or third watch of the night and finds them alert, those servants will be blessed.” (Luke 12:38). Late hours don't change it. What counts is that they're alert when he comes.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, “Even if he comes in the second or third watch of the night and finds them alert, those servants will be blessed.” (Luke 12:38). A late arrival doesn't take the blessing away. The alert servants are still blessed.

It's actually the other way around, baker. Jesus says, “If the homeowner had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into.” (Luke 12:39). Knowing the hour would have let him stop it. That's the point of the picture: the Son of Man “…will come at an hour you do not expect.” so stay ready (Luke 12:40).

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “You also must be ready…” (Luke 12:40). It's the same call He opened with, dressed for service and lamps burning. Ready is the whole message here.
That's the word, friend. Jesus says the Son of Man “…will come at an hour you do not expect.” (Luke 12:40). So nobody gets to plan around it. That's why He says to be ready.

Quiet would be peaceful, baker, but it's not in the verse. Jesus says, “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.” (Luke 12:40). He's asking for ready, not silent. Nobody was told to whisper.

Fear is a strong word, friend, but it's not the one Jesus uses here. He says, “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.” (Luke 12:40). The word is ready, and the other blank is expect. He's telling them to be prepared.

Rich would be nice, baker, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.” (Luke 12:40). Money never comes up in this verse. Ready is what He asks for.

explanations.answer: Whether it's for them or everyone
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples, asks, “Lord, are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (Luke 12:41). He wants to know who's meant to hear it. That's a good question to ask out loud.

explanations.answer: When the master will come back
explanations.explanation: That one's not Peter's question, friend. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples, asks, “Lord, are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (Luke 12:41). He's asking who the parable is for. The hour is something Jesus has just said will come when you don't expect it (Luke 12:40).

explanations.answer: Which servant the master will reward
explanations.explanation: Close to the topic, baker, but it's not what Peter asks. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples, says, “Lord, are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (Luke 12:41). His question is about who the parable is for. Rewards aren't part of what he asks.

explanations.answer: Give them their portion on time
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Jesus says the master puts the manager in charge of his servants “…to give them their portion at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). So the job is to get everyone their share when it's due. Faithful and wise means doing that.

No tenants or rent in these verses, baker. Jesus says the master puts the manager in charge of his servants “…to give them their portion at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). The manager gives out the portions. He isn't out collecting.

explanations.answer: Keep count of the master's flocks
explanations.explanation: There are no flocks in this passage, friend, so there's nothing to count. Jesus says the manager is in charge of the master's servants “…to give them their portion at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). That's the job: portions, given on time.

True, baker. Jesus says, “Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.” (Luke 12:43-44). Faithful work gets a big reward. That's the master's answer to a job done well.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, “Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.” (Luke 12:43-44). The faithful manager is blessed, and he's trusted with everything the master owns.

explanations.answer: His master will be a long time coming
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, baker. Jesus says the servant says in his heart, “…‘My master will be a long time in coming,’…” (Luke 12:45). It's the 'no rush, he's not here yet' kind of thinking. It's a lot like telling yourself 'I'll just rest my eyes' while the oven timer is running.

explanations.answer: His master will be home before dawn
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says, friend. This servant says in his heart, “…‘My master will be a long time in coming,’…” (Luke 12:45). He's thinking his master is far off, not close. Nothing in the verse mentions dawn.

explanations.answer: His master will send a messenger first
explanations.explanation: A heads up would be nice, baker, but that's not in the verse. This servant says in his heart, “…‘My master will be a long time in coming,’…” (Luke 12:45). A messenger never comes up. He's assuming the master is a long way off.

The one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment gets “…few blows.” (Luke 12:48). I think this is a heavy one, and the text is clear that knowing the master's will matters.
